prompt_topic: sacubitril/valsartan (angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition) in heart failure
raw_text:
Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health challenge characterized by high morbidity, mortality, and economic burden. The introduction of sacubitril/valsartan, a first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), represented a major paradigm shift in HF management [1]. Sacubitril/valsartan exhibits a dual mechanism of action: sacubitril is a prodrug that, upon activation, inhibits the enzyme neprilysin, thereby preventing the degradation of beneficial vasoactive peptides such as natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin; concurrently, valsartan selectively blocks the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor to suppress the deleterious vasoconstrictive and sodium-retaining effects of angiotensin II [2]. This combined neurohormonal approach promotes vasodilation, natriuresis, and diuresis while preventing cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis [1,2].

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established the superiority of sacubitril/valsartan over the standard-of-care angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor enalapril in patients with chronic HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [1]. In this trial, sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20% compared to enalapril [1]. Further analysis confirmed that this clinical benefit extended to halting overall disease progression, reducing the requirement for intensive therapies, and decreasing emergency department visits [2]. To address the safety and efficacy of initiating ARNI therapy during acute decompensation, the PIONEER-HF trial randomized hospitalized HFrEF patients after hemodynamic stabilization [3]. PIONEER-HF demonstrated a significantly greater reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) concentration in the sacubitril/valsartan group compared to the enalapril group [3], along with a substantial reduction in the risk of serious post-discharge clinical events [4]. Crucially, the TRANSITION trial confirmed that early initiation of sacubitril/valsartan in hospitalized HFrEF patients—either prior to or shortly after discharge—was clinically feasible, safe, and well-tolerated, avoiding unnecessary delays in optimizing guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) [5].

Mechanistic evaluations have provided deep insights into the structural benefits of ARNI therapy. The PROVE-HF trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan therapy is associated with rapid and significant cardiac reverse remodeling, as evidenced by a reduction in left ventricular volumes and an increase in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), which strongly correlated with decreases in NT-proBNP [6]. Concurrently, the EVALUATE-HF trial compared sacubitril/valsartan to enalapril, demonstrating a significant early reduction in left atrial volume index and improved markers of cardiac structure and function, although changes in aortic stiffness did not differ significantly [7]. Beyond physiological parameters, sacubitril/valsartan significantly improves patient-reported outcomes. In the PARADIGM-HF trial, patients receiving sacubitril/valsartan experienced better health-related quality of life, measured via the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ), compared to those on enalapril [8]. Real-world validation from the CHAMP-HF registry confirmed that initiating sacubitril/valsartan is associated with rapid, sustained, and clinically meaningful improvements in health status outside of clinical trial settings [9].

Given its outstanding success in HFrEF, sacubitril/valsartan was subsequently evaluated across a broader spectrum of LVEF. The PARAGON-HF trial compared sacubitril/valsartan with valsartan alone in patients with heart failure and preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF; LVEF $\ge$ 45%) [10]. Although the trial narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death and total HF hospitalizations, subgroup analyses revealed significant clinical benefits in patients with lower-range ejection fractions (45–57%) and in women [10]. A pooled analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF confirmed that the therapeutic benefit of sacubitril/valsartan extends across the LVEF spectrum, particularly benefiting patients with mildly reduced LVEF (HFmrEF) up to an ejection fraction of approximately 55–60% [11,12]. To further investigate this, the PARAGLIDE-HF trial evaluated sacubitril/valsartan in patients with stabilized acute decompensated HF and LVEF > 40%, showing a significant reduction in NT-proBNP and suggesting a benefit in this broader population [13].

Cardiorenal protection is another clinical hallmark of ARNI therapy. In HFrEF, sacubitril/valsartan significantly slowed the decline of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and reduced the rate of renal events compared to enalapril [14]. This preservation of renal function was consistent across different baseline levels of kidney function [15], and was particularly pronounced in patients with comorbid type 2 diabetes [16]. Furthermore, post-hoc analyses of PARADIGM-HF showed that patients treated with sacubitril/valsartan had significantly better glycemic control over time, with a greater reduction in HbA1c compared to those on enalapril [17]. In the HFpEF population, PARAGON-HF also demonstrated a reduced risk of renal events with sacubitril/valsartan compared to valsartan [18]. In terms of long-term safety, the PERSPECTIVE trial successfully addressed theoretical concerns regarding neprilysin-mediated beta-amyloid accumulation in the brain, demonstrating that long-term sacubitril/valsartan therapy does not adversely affect cognitive function [19]. However, in advanced HF (NYHA class IV), the LIFE trial revealed that sacubitril/valsartan did not offer a significant benefit in NT-proBNP reduction or clinical outcomes compared to valsartan, highlighting limitations in the most severe stages of the disease [20].

The utility of ARNI has also been explored in acute myocardial infarction (MI). The PARADISE-MI trial compared sacubitril/valsartan with ramipril in patients post-MI with reduced LVEF or pulmonary congestion; however, it did not show a statistically significant reduction in the primary composite endpoint [21]. In terms of safety, although symptomatic hypotension is more common with sacubitril/valsartan, rates of severe hyperkalemia [22] and renal dysfunction are low, and the efficacy of the drug remains robust across different background doses of beta-blockers [23]. Furthermore, ARNI treatment reduces microalbuminuria [24] and significantly lowers the risk of sudden cardiac death [25].

Consequently, major professional societies, including the ACC/AHA/HFSA [26] and the ESC [27], recommend ARNI as a Class I, first-line foundation of GDMT for HFrEF. This is supported by comprehensive modeling estimating that a quadruple regimen including ARNI, SGLT2 inhibitors, beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists offers substantial lifetime survival benefits [28,29]. Finally, health economics analyses have confirmed that sacubitril/valsartan is highly cost-effective, cementing its role as a cornerstone of modern heart failure therapy [30].
